title: Ignatius to the Magnesians
subtitle: one overseer, one altar, and no going back: 'no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day]'
lead: At Smyrna, on his way under guard to die in Rome, Ignatius of Antioch met four leaders of the church of Magnesia, a city a few hours from Ephesus: the young overseer Damas, two elders and a deacon. He wrote back to their church. The letter asks it to stay united with its overseer, who presides 'in the place of God', and with its elders, 'in the place of the council of the apostles' (6:1), so that there is 'one temple of God ... one altar ... one Jesus Christ' (7:2).

Its second half warns against living 'by Judaism' (8:1), and holds two of the most quoted lines in early Christian writing: 'If, then, those who lived in the old ways came to a new hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day] ...' (9:1), and 'Christianity did not put its faith in Judaism. Judaism put its faith in Christianity' (10:3), the first known uses of the word 'Christianity' (Lightfoot). No church counts the letter as Scripture; it is read here as an early witness, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.

Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome. Eusebius names the letter, 'to the church in Magnesia on the Maeander, where again he made mention of the overseer Damas' (Church History 3.36.5).

Written at Smyrna (15:1) on the journey to Rome. None of these four letters is dated; To the Romans, written there too, ends 'I write this to you on the 24th of August' (Lake's English; Ignatius to the Romans 10:3). Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.' (as Lake reports it); Lake: 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Smyrna, with the Ephesian delegates and Polycarp (15:1)
The church at Magnesia on the Maeander, in the Roman province of Asia, with its overseer Damas, the elders Bassus and Apollonius and the deacon Zotion (2:1)
Letter of thanks and warning from a condemned prisoner
Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension: the Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), the long recension (g), and the Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus' (1:0), a prisoner in chains (1:2; 12:1) whose church is in Syria (14:1). Eusebius knew it as one of the four letters written at Smyrna and names its overseer, Damas (Church History 3.36.5). Polycarp, who is named in 15:1, sent copies of Ignatius's letters to Philippi: 'we have sent you the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us, and the others we had here with us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).

The seven letters survive in three forms: a long recension with interpolations and added letters, the short (middle) recension of the seven Eusebius names, which Lake follows, and a Syriac abridgment of three letters that does not include To the Magnesians (Lake). In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius'. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again: Sergio Zañartu's survey (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), R. Joly (1979), J. Rius-Camps (1980), R. M. Hübner (1997) and T. Lechner (1999) among those who argued that the letters, or some of them, are later; Zañartu himself holds to the short recension's authenticity until the contrary is proved. B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment. Fritz Guy (1964) wrote that 'The conclusions of Zahn and Lightfoot have since been accepted by practically all scholars'.

audience.to: The church at Magnesia on the Maeander, about fifteen Roman miles from Ephesus (Lightfoot), which had sent its overseer Damas, the elders Bassus and Apollonius and the deacon Zotion to meet Ignatius at Smyrna (2:1). Its overseer was young (3:1). Some, Ignatius says, called him overseer but did everything without him (4:1), and some teachers urged living 'by Judaism' and denied Christ's death (8:1; 9:1), though Ignatius says he does not know that any Magnesians are 'like this' (11:1).
audience.why: To thank the church for its delegates (Lake: the immediate purpose of each letter but Romans 'is to thank the recipients for the kindness which they had shown to Ignatius'), to bind it to its young overseer, elders and deacons (2-7; 13), to guard it in advance against a teaching that kept the old practices and denied the reality of Christ's death (8-11), and to ask prayer for Antioch (14). Knowing that he writes to a church not yet touched by the teaching explains why the warnings come with praise.
views: Lake: 'it is disputed whether he means that this was an evil found in docetic circles, or that it was a danger threatening the church from other directions.' Lightfoot: 'The heresy therefore is a Docetic Judaism.' Fritz Guy (1964): 'Judaizing' here is 'an inner, spiritual attitude' more than ritual.

outline: Greeting to the church in Magnesia
Why I write: union of flesh and spirit
The young overseer and the overseer of all
The overseer in the place of God
Not by Judaism; the Word from silence
Living by the Lord's day; the prophets raised
The new yeast; Christianity and Judaism
Truly and surely, under Pontius Pilate
Pray for the church in Syria

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: Magnesia and its delegates, a young overseer, who the teachers of 'Judaism' were, what keeping the Sabbath and 'the Lord's' meant to Christians in Asia in Ignatius's day, and the witnesses where they differ (8:2; 9:1).

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: Paul's 'Judaism' and 'live in the Jewish way' (Galatians 1:13-14; 2:14), the old yeast (1 Corinthians 5:7), days and the Lord's day (Colossians 2:16-17; Revelation 1:10), the Son who does nothing on his own (John 5:19), the coin (Matthew 22:19), and the Word (John 1:1).

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the questions churches still ask of it: the overseer 'in the place of God', the elders and deacons (6:1; 13:1-2), 'valid' meetings (4:1), and the Lord's day against the Sabbath (9:1), each church's reading from its own documents.

sections.h: From Smyrna, to a church that came to meet him
sections.b: Eusebius tells that at Smyrna, 'where Polycarp was', Ignatius wrote one letter to the church in Ephesus, 'another to the one in Magnesia on the Maeander, where again he made mention of the overseer Damas', and another to Tralles (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot follows Strabo's road: Magnesia is the first city after Ephesus, Tralles the next. Magnesia had sent a delegation that, in Lightfoot's words, 'comprised all orders of the ministry' (2:1), and Ignatius writes 'in acknowledgement of the attention' it showed him.

sections.h: The young overseer and the order of the church
sections.b: Damas was young (3:1). Ignatius asks the church not to take advantage of that, and builds the whole first half on unity with him: the overseer presides 'in the place of God', the elders 'in the place of the council of the apostles', the deacons serve Christ (6:1); 'do nothing without the overseer and the elders' (7:1). Catholic teaching cites 6:1 for the bishop as 'like the living image of God the Father' (Catechism 1549); Lightfoot called the letters' language an 'extravagant exaltation of the episcopal office' explained by 'the needs and distractions of the age'. The site's cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3 give each church's teaching on bishops and elders.

The second half warns against 'other opinions' and 'old myths', and against living 'by Judaism' (8:1), with Paul's own words (Galatians 1:13-14; 2:14). Ignatius sets the prophets on Christ's side: they 'lived by Christ Jesus' and were persecuted for it (8:2), and Christ 'raised them from the dead' (9:2). Who held the teaching he opposes is debated (see the book's audience and the note at 10:3). The letter is written to Christians about a practice among Christians; the site's topic Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible gives the later history of Christian texts used against Jews.

sections.h: The Sabbath and the Lord's day
sections.b: Chapter 9 is the passage quoted most from this letter: 'If, then, those who lived in the old ways came to a new hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day], on which our life also rose through him and through his death, which some deny ...' (9:1). It is the first half of a condition; the second half is the question 'how will we be able to live without him?' (9:2). Its text is uncertain at one word: the Greek has no word for 'day' (the brackets mark the supplied word), and the Greek manuscript adds 'life'. Its subject is argued: Jewish believers (Lightfoot) or the prophets (Fritz Guy). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it for Sunday replacing the Sabbath's 'ceremonial observance' (Catechism 2175). Fritz Guy concluded that it 'can not at the present time properly be introduced as evidence' that the Lord's day was kept. See the chapter page, the views note at 9:1, and the cards at Revelation 1:10, Exodus 20 and Colossians 2.

In 8:2 Lake prints 'his Word, who came forth from silence', the reading of the Armenian and of Severus of Antioch; the Greek manuscript and the Latin read 'his eternal Word, not coming forth from silence'. Lake, with 'recent editors', takes the longer reading for 'a doctrinal emendation due to fear of Gnostic theories'. Lightfoot, who first argued for the shorter reading in 1868, reads it of the incarnation: God's silence broken by his Word.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the young overseer and the old ways
spec.body: The letter has two problems, a young overseer some did not take seriously (3:1; 4:1) and teachers of 'old myths' and the 'old ways' (8:1; 9:1). Ignatius may have joined them on purpose: against a young leader, an appeal to what is old carries weight. His answer turns the ages around. The 'old' yeast has gone sour (10:2), those who lived in the old ways came to 'a new hope' (9:1), and the young overseer stands for the Father who 'was with' the Son 'before the ages' (6:1). This is my reading of the letter's structure.

prompts:
On a stone quay at Smyrna, a chained bearded prisoner between two Roman soldiers greets four travelers in dusty cloaks: a young man with a staff, two older men and a deacon carrying a satchel; behind them the road winds back through hills toward a valley with a river.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

canon.summary: Ignatius to the Magnesians is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is honored by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, and the Catholic Catechism quotes this letter on the bishop (1549) and on Sunday (2175).
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' calendar keeps 17 October as the Memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catechism cites this letter at 1549 (with To the Trallians) and quotes 9:1 at 2175.

Not part of the Bible: Reid (1908) states that the Eastern Orthodox churches 'have a New Testament identical with the Catholic'. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.

Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar keeps 17 October as a Lesser Festival of 'Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, Martyr, c.107'.
Commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October, and says he 'was the first to use the word catholic to describe the universality of the Church'.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.h: Smyrna, on the way to Rome
provenance.b: Ignatius wrote at Smyrna, with the Ephesian delegates and Polycarp beside him (15:1). Eusebius lists it second of the four letters from Smyrna (Church History 3.36.5).

In the Greek Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), in the long recension (g), and in Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions (Lake). The Syriac abridgment of three letters does not include it (Lake). In the long recension, Guy notes, chapter 9 'is about three times as long' as in the short.

rejected_why.h: A bishop's letter, not an apostle's
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius writes 'as one less than you' (11:1) and asks the Magnesians to stand firm 'in the decrees of the Lord and of the apostles' (13:1), setting the apostles above himself; in To the Romans he says, 'They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3).

rejected_why.h: Treated as a letter of a church writer
rejected_why.b: Eusebius describes the letters in his history (Church History 3.36) and does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25).

cited_in.b: John's 'the Lord's day' (hē kyriakē hēmera) and Ignatius's 'the Lord's' (kyriakē, with no word for day) use the same adjective. The New Testament does not quote this letter.
Paul's verb 'live in the Jewish way' (ioudaizein) is the one Ignatius uses; 'Judaism' (Ioudaismos) is Paul's word in Galatians 1:13-14.
The old yeast and the new, in Lake's margin; Ignatius makes Christ the new yeast.
'To go to his own place', in Lake's margin.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to church life in Asia early in the second century the letter is of the first importance: one overseer with elders and deacons in a small city's church, a warning against living 'by Judaism', a much-quoted line on the Sabbath and 'the Lord's', and the earliest known uses of the word 'Christianity' (Lightfoot). Its text rests on one medieval Greek manuscript with versions, and at the two places that matter most to later readers (8:2; 9:1) the witnesses differ. Its historical claims are few and fit Eusebius. In doctrine it follows the New Testament on Christ; its rules on the overseer go beyond anything the New Testament says.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows a church with an overseer, elders and deacons (2:1; 13:1), people who called him overseer but did everything without him (4:1), a teaching that kept the old practices and denied Christ's death (8:1; 9:1), Christians confessing Christ's birth, suffering and resurrection 'in the time when Pontius Pilate was governor' (11:1), and Christians who could be said to 'live by the Lord's day' (9:1).

Fair. Only one Greek manuscript of the short recension survives, the Medicean, which Guy dates to the eleventh century, with Latin, Armenian and Syriac versions. At 8:2 the Greek and Latin have a reading Lake and Lightfoot judge a doctrinal change; at 9:1 the Greek adds 'life', which Lake leaves out. The Plain English Translation follows Lake throughout and gives the differences in the variants.

The letter claims to be by Ignatius, writing from Smyrna (15:1), and names Damas, Bassus, Apollonius and Zotion (2:1) and Polycarp (15:1). Eusebius knew it and names Damas (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot, of the overseers the letters name: 'Under any circumstances it seems probable that these were not fictitious personages, for, even if he were a forger, he would be anxious to give an air of reality to his writings' (The Christian Ministry, page 50). The genuineness of the seven letters was long debated, and the debate was renewed in the twentieth century: the authorship section gives the views and who holds them.

Matches: the Son who does nothing on his own (7:1; John 5:19), who came from the Father and returns to him (7:2; John 16:28), born, suffering and raised under Pontius Pilate (11:1; 1 Timothy 6:13); the old and new yeast (10:2; 1 Corinthians 5:7); the prophets who foretold Christ by his Spirit (8:2; 9:2; 1 Peter 1:10-11); Father, Son and Spirit named together (13:1; Matthew 28:19). Goes beyond: the overseer 'in the place of God' and the rule to 'do nothing without the overseer and the elders' (6:1; 7:1) have no parallel in the New Testament, where the elders of Ephesus are called overseers (Acts 20:17, 28) and Philippi has several overseers (Philippians 1:1); 'raised them from the dead' (9:2) takes a step past 1 Peter 3:19 and Matthew 27:52. In tension: Ignatius's contrast of Christianity and Judaism (10:3) is sharper than Paul's, who says of Israel that 'they are beloved, for the sake of the patriarchs' and that 'God does not take back his gifts and his call' (Romans 11:28-29). On the Sabbath and Sunday, where the churches differ, see the cards at Revelation 1:10 and Colossians 2:16-17.

how_to_read.h: As a thank-you letter with a warning
how_to_read.b: Read 1-7 as the call to unity and 8-11 as its reason: unity with the overseer is the guard against the teaching Ignatius fears. Remember that he says he does not know that any Magnesians hold it (11:1).
At 8:2 and 9:1 the reading changes the sense. Read the variant entries before quoting either verse.

how_to_read.h: As a witness the churches read differently
how_to_read.b: Catholic teaching quotes 6:1 and 9:1 (Catechism 1549; 2175). Churches differ on bishops and on the day of worship: the notes point to the site's cards on the 66 books.
